turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Um, well, I came in today because... lately I've had to be a lot more out in front of people at work. I plan events, so I'm around crowds and cameras a lot. And I just can't stop staring at this one uneven-looking part of my face, especially in photos. It's really bothering me. Everyone else tells me they barely see anything when I point it out, but... I just can't stop focusing on it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived unevenness in their face that others say is barely noticeable.

turns.doctor_question: When you are feeling self-conscious about this part of your face, do you find yourself doing anything specific to try to hide it or check it in the mirror?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do. Um, especially before I send out event pictures or have to jump into a vendor meeting. I'll just keep checking my face in my phone camera. I end up retaking photos a bunch of times, or I'll make sure to tilt my head a certain way so it doesn't look as obvious. 

And sometimes I'll just ask a coworker if I look weird, just to see what they say. It... it actually eats up a lot of my time, honestly. Enough that I sometimes fall behind on my actual planning stuff because I'm so caught up in checking how I look.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors such as checking their face in the camera, retaking photos, tilting their head to hide the perceived flaw, and seeking reassurance from coworkers.

turns.doctor_question: When you look at your face and see this unevenness, do you feel that your reaction to it is out of proportion to how it actually looks, or are you convinced that it is a genuine, visible defect that others should be able to see?
turns.patient_response:
I'm honestly not sure. I mean... to me, it looks incredibly obvious. I see it right away when I look at a picture or in the mirror, and I feel like it's this glaring thing that everyone must be staring at. 

But then, like I said, people tell me they barely see anything at all. So... I guess part of me thinks maybe I am blowing it out of proportion, since no one else seems to notice it like I do. But when I'm actually looking at it, it just feels so real and noticeable to me. I really don't know what to think anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a perceived glaring defect in their face that others tell them they barely see, confirming a preoccupation with a flaw that appears slight to others.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from checking in the mirror or asking others for reassurance, do you find yourself mentally comparing your face to others or dwelling on how you 'should' look for long periods of time?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, not really. I don't think I do that. I don't really look at other people and compare my face to theirs. It's... it's really just my own face that I'm focused on. And I don't sit around thinking about how I'm supposed to look, exactly. I just... I just want this one specific part to not look so uneven. So, no, I don't really spend time comparing myself to anyone else.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient states she is focused on her own face and wants a specific part to not look 'uneven', indicating a preoccupation with a perceived physical flaw.
